English Description: The characteristics depending of age and sex of the bird. Although there are slight variations between different subspecies of A. cyanoptera, they tend to share common traits nonetheless. The color of the adult male's head, chest, and underside is generally purple-chestnut, and the abdomen is dark brown. The lower back and rear of the bird are greenish-brown, while the wing coverts are blue. There are variations in shoulder feather color between birds, ranging from yellow with a center stripe, to green with a center stripe. The juvenile is similar in appearance to the adult female, having a green speculum with a white leading edge, and pale blue upper secondary coverts. The adult male's basic markings are similar to these, but he has red eyes and a brighter forewing. From the fall to the spring, the adult male has an alternate plumage. The head, neck, belly, and flanks are bright red, while the back is dark brown. Additionally, the male has black under tail coverts in the fall through spring time span. (Gammonley, 1996) (Cadwell, M. 2002. "Anas cyanoptera" (On-line), Animal Diversity Web. Accessed December 11, 2012 at http://animaldiversity.ummz.umich.edu/accounts/Anas_cyanoptera/).

English Description: It is a medium sized bird, length range from 20 to 36 cm, its weight varies from 340 and 360 g. Beak blackish with white base, legs reddish or pink, amber eyes in adult and dark in juveniles. No sexual dimorphism present. The head is commonly dark and green-purple iridescent. The original color pattern is light gray with two large black bars on the wings, a black band at the tip of the tail and a white rump. Currently, most of individuals vary in color, from completely white and red irregular spots to black with white tail. When they are associated to a large number in urban areas they become pests capable of transmitting disease, contaminate food and cause damage to structures that generate large economic losses, they are called "flying rats". In the wild they live between 5-15 years and in captivity they can live longer

Comúnmente la cabeza es oscura y presenta una iridiscencia verde-púrpura. El patrón original de color es gris claro con dos grandes franjas de color negro en las alas, una franja negra en la punta de la cola y la rabadilla blanca. Actualmente la mayor parte de los individuos son de otros colores, desde blanco total o con manchas irregulares rojizas hasta negro con plumas primarias y cola blanca. English Description: It measures 30-3 6cm and weights some 100 g; males are slightly larger than females. Smooth-billed anis have an even black plumage with iridescent specles in neck and nape. The beak is laterally compressed, the culmen resembles a blade. Unlike other members of this genus, it does not have furrows or protuberances in the bill. Its wings are short and the tail is long. Legs, feet, beak and iris are black. Males and females look alike. Juveniles have dull blackish plumage, smaller and straight beaks (until approx. age of 9 month). Smooth-billed anis is social, forming groups that range in size from 8 to 25 individuals. Groups of up to 60 individuals have been registered for Galapagos. Smooth-billed anis has a complex vocal system including five different calls: contact, alarm, gathering, threat and high-pitch alarm.
Spanish Description: Mide entre 30 y 36 cm de longitud y pesa unos 100 gr; los machos son ligeramente más grandes que las hembras. El pico es comprimido lateralmente, el culmen forma una afilada cresta similar a una cuchilla, a diferencia de los otros miembros de su género, no presenta surcos ni protuberancias. Tiene alas cortas y cola larga. Las patas, pico e iris son negros. Es una especie social, forma grupos que van de ocho a 25 aves,  incluso se ha visto grupos de hasta de 60 aves. No presentan dimorfismo sexual marcado, los machos adultos son ligeramente más grandes que las hembras. El tamaño del pico es un buen parámetro para diferenciar los sexos, los juveniles tienen el pico casi recto, sin el arco típico y permanecen así hasta los 9 meses de edad. Estudios determinaron que los anis tienen un sistema complejo de vocalizaciones o llamados, se identificaron cinco. Un llamado de comunicación, uno de Alarma, el llamado para ir a dormir, el de amenaza y un grito que usan cuando están muy asustados.

English Description: They are gregarious birds of medium size, capable of performing short flights. They have a distinctive social system and a hierarchical order established: there is a dominant male and a male subjected by all. Females have a separate hierarchy without dominance of males. Sexual dimorphism is evident at plain sight in this genus, the males are larger (50 cm.), they weigh up to 4 kg with two types of caruncular bumps on the head: a crest on the pileus and a pair of lobes which hang on both sides of the beak. The tail is composed of large, arching feathers. Two white spots on the cheeks make the difference between closely related species. It has gray legs, which are fitted with spurs in some races, but this is absent in the females. The hens are smaller, measuring no more than 40 cm and weighing about 2 kg. Its coloration is less striking, the fleshy appendages of the head are smaller, the tail is shorter. Life span depends on race, it could go from five to ten years.
Spanish Description: Son aves gregarias, de tamaño mediano, capaces de realizar vuelos cortos. Con un sistema social característico y un orden jerárquico establecido, hay un macho dominante y un macho sometido por todos. Las hembras tienen un orden jerárquico independiente sin dominancia de los machos. El dimorfismo sexual es evidente a simple vista en éste género, los machos son más grandes (50cm) llegan a pesar hasta 4 kg, con dos tipos de protuberancias carunculares en la cabeza, una cresta en el píleo y un par de lóbulos que cuelgan a ambos lados del pico. La cola está compuesta por plumas grandes y arqueadas. Dos manchas blancas en las mejillas marcan la diferencia entre especies cercanas. Posee patas grisáceas, que en algunas razas están provistas de espolones, esto es ausente en las hembras. Las gallinas son más pequeñas, no miden más de 40 cm y pesan unos 2 kg, su coloración es menos llamativa, los apéndices carnosos de la cabeza son más pequeños, la cola es más corta. El tiempo de vida depende de la raza, pude ir de cinco a diez años.

Como las principales especies de insectívoros, tal vez está siendo afectado por el uso de pesticidas, también es afectado por el parásito Plasmodium y por la mosca Philornis downsi que puede causar alta mortalidad de pichones.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: The only bright yellow bird with a bright, sweet song. Together with the population from the Coco islands, it is considered a sub-species (Setophaga petechia aureola) characterized by the brown-reddish cap on its head.  Genetic divergence is low. Probably colonized the archipelago less than 300 000 yrs ago.
Spanish Description: Es el único pájaro amarillo brillante de las islas. Tal como la población de las islas Coco, ésta se considera como una sub-especie distinta (Setophaga petechia aureola). Tiene como característica una gorra rojiza-café en la cabeza. Existe poca diferencia genética con poblaciones del continente y se estima que llegó a las islas hace menos de 300 000 años.

Author: (Forster, JR, 1772)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Dendroica striata Forster, JR, 1772
Distribution Comments: There is a single record of a male bird netted on 16 May 1976 on Daphne Major.

Author: (Snodgras & Heller, 1901)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Cactospiza heliobates (Snodgras & Heller, 1901); Geospiza heliobates Snodgras & Heller, 1901
Distribution Comments: Present on Playa Tortuga Negra, Caleta Black and Cartago on Isabela Island. Extinct on Fernandina.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente en Playa Tortuga Negra, Caleta Negra y Cartago en Isabela. Extinct on Fernandina.
English Comments: Threats: The species is threatened by the loss of habitats, mangrove are very restricted habitats on the Galápagos, rats, but the main current threat is probably the introduced fly Philornis downsi that causes high chick mortality of that small clutch species. Annual survey are performed and a captive breeding program (head starting) was started to try to support the populations while control of Philornis is still not possible. Head starting means collecting eggs, hand rearing chicks and return them into their original habitat once independent.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas: La especie es amenazada por la pérdida de hábitat, el manglar es un ambiente muy restringido en las Galápagos. La rata introducida es otra de las amenazas, pero quizá la mayor amenaza actual es la mosca introducida Philornis downsi que causa alta mortalidad de pichones en una especie con tan pequeña población. Los estudios que se llevan a cabo anualmente y un programa de crianza en cautiverio (ahora en proceso de inicio) están en el camino de mejorar la población, mientras que aun no es posible el control de Philornis. Se trata de colectar huevos, incubar y criar los pichones, y volverlos a su sitio de origen cuando están independientes.
Información adicional Venegas, L.

Author: Sclater & Salvin, 1870
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Cactornis pallida Sclater & Salvin, 1870; Cactospiza pallida; Camarhynchus pallidus pallidus (Sclater & Salvin, 1870); Camarhynchus pallidus productus Ridgway, 1894; Camarhynchus pallidus striatipecta (Swarth, 1931)
Distribution Comments: Breeds on Isabela, Fernandina (probably), Santa Cruz, Santiago, San Cristóbal, and Pinzón (rarely). It has also been recorded on Rábida (specimens 1897 and 1905), Floreana (specimen 1905) and Santa Fe (two sight records 1968), and a sight record on Pinta in 1968.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Anida en Isabela, Fernandina (probable), Santa Cruz, Santiago, San Cristóbal y Pinzón (raro). Existe registros antiguos en Rábida (1897 y 1905), Floreana (1905),  Santa Fe (visto 2 veces 1968), y una observación en Pinta en 1968.
English Comments:
Threats
Like other finches, current threats are mainly from diseases and parasites. Is known to be affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality. Highland birds that contracted pox in captivity, were heavily affected by this disease.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Como otros pinzones, las amenazas son mayormente enfermedades y parásitos, se conoce que es afectado por la mosca parasita Philornis downsi que produce alta mortalidad de pichones. En estudios previos realizados en Santa Cruz, los individuos de la parte alta que contrajeron Viruela Aviar en cautiverio fueron fuertemente afectados por enfermedades.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: Black during reproduction, olive-light brown colour outside the breeding season and pinkish when young. Males and females look alike, with upper parts olive to warm brown with little streaking and underparts creamy to yellowish with slight streaking on upper breast. Males in San Cristóbal can get a black hood  blackish plumage was observed in approximately a fifth of the San Cristóbal population.
Spanish Description: El pico  negro durante la reproducción, café olivo brillante fuera de la época reproductiva y los jóvenes de color rosáceo. Machos y hembras son parecidos, partes superiores de olivas a café cálido con pocas estrías y partes bajas de cremoso a amarillento con finas estrías en el pecho alto. Los machos en San Cristóbal pueden tener una capucha de plumaje negruzco, lo ha sido observado en aproximadamente la mitad de la población de esta isla.

Author: (Gould, 1837)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Camarhynchus parvulus parvulus (Gould 1837); Camarhynchus parvulus salvini Ridgway 1894; Geospiza parvulus (Gould, 1837); Camarhynchus prosthemelas (Schlater & Salvin, 1870).
Distribution Comments: Found on Isabela, Fernandina, Santa Cruz, Santiago, San Cristobal, Floreana, Baltra, Santa Fe, Pinzon y Rabida. Has been seen on Pinta but it is not known if there isa breeding population there. Found mostly in the highlands and the transitional zone.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Encuentra en Isabela, Fernandina, Santa Cruz, Santiago, San Cristobal, Floreana, Baltra, Santa Fe, Pinzon y Rabida. Tambien se puede observar en Pinta pero no se sabe si se reproduce en esta isla. Común en la parte alta y zona de transición.
English Comments:
Threats
Known to be affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality. Recent studies showed very low breeding success that may cause long term population collapse.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Se conoce que está afectada por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi la que causa alta mortalidad de pichones. Recientes estudios muestran un muy bajo éxito reproductivo que puede causar un colapso de su población a largo plazo.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: Smallest of the Darwin tree finches, 13 gr average, same as small ground finch. Short conical beak. Males develop a black hood with age, starting with face and head, while upper parts are olive green and underparts creamy. Males in San Cristóbal hardly ever have black plumage, but upper breast is heavily streaked. Females and young males have green-olive upper parts and creamy to yellowish underparts.
Spanish Description: Es el pinzón de árbol más pequeño, 13g como el pinzón pequeño de tierra.  Pico corto cónico. La cabeza de los machos se pone negra con la edad, la espalda verde oliva y el vientre más crema. Los machos de San Cristóbal casi nunca se ponen negros, pero tienen la parte superior del pecho más rayada. Hembras y juveniles con  espalda verde oliva y el vientre más crema amarillento.

Author: Ridgway, 1890
Distribution Comments: Present on Floreana Island.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente en Floreana.
English Comments:
Threats
Threats are similar to all other finches, particularly very low nesting success due to the introduced parasitic fly Philornis downsi: the flies lay the eggs in the nest and larvae suck the blood of the nestlings, causing anaemia, lesions and consequently nestling mortality. There is predation by the introduced black rat. The impact of diseases is unknown.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Las amenazas son similares a las de todos los otros pinzones, particularmente bajo éxito reproductivo debido a la mosca parásita introducida Philornis downsi: las moscas ponen huevos dentro del nido y las larvas succionan la sangre de los pichones, causando anemia, lesiones y en consecuencia la mortalidad de los pichones. Hay depredación por parte de la rata negra introducida y se desconoce si hay impactos por enfermedades.
Información adicional Venegas, L.

Author: Gould, 1837
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Camarhynchus psittaculus Gould, 1841; Camarhynchus psittacula affinis Ridgway, 1894; Camarhynchus psittacula habeli Sclater & Salvin, 1870; Camarhynchus psittacula psittacula Gould, 1837; Camarhynchus habeli Sclater & Salvin, 1870.
Distribution Comments: The species is found on all the main islands except Española, Genovesa, Wolf and Darwin. It does not now breed on Santa Fe, although observations continued until 1968. It is extinct on Pinzón, where it was last seen in 1906.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Casi en todas las islas excepto Española, Genovesa, Wolf and Darwin. Ha desaparecido de Santa Fé (última observación 1968) y Pinzón.
English Comments:
Threats
It iIs known to be affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality. There is no information on impact of pox and other diseases; might be sensitive to habitat changes related to human activities.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Se conoce que se encuentra afectada por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi que causa alta mortalidad de pichones. No existe información sobre el impacto de viruela aviar y otras enfermedades; podría ser sensible a cambios en el hábitat relacionados con actividades humanas.
Información adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: This is the largest and heaviest bodied of the tree-finch species, 18 g average. Medium long and heavy, parrot like beak, approximately as long as deep.
Spanish Description: Es el pinzón de árbol más grande y pesado, con approx. 18g. Tiene un pico grueso casi tan alto como largo, un poco curvo, similar a un pico de loro.

Author: Sclater & Salvin, 1870
Taxonomic Comments:
This species is closely related to the Green Warbler Finch, and were formerly considered conspecific, but both species differed in appearance, distribution, habitat, and song. Syn.: Certhidea olivacea Gould, 1837.
A recent genetic study has shown a single colonization event about 850 000 yrs ago from southern central America rather than continental Ecuador.
Distribution Comments: C. fusca is found on the smaller islands in the north, east and south of the archipelago, practically spanning the entire length of the archipelago. Present on Darwin, Wolf, Española, Santa Fe, San Cristobal, Pinta, Floreana.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente en las pequeñas islas del norte, este y sur del archipiélago, Darwin, Wolf, Española, Santa Fe, San Cristobal, Pinta y Floreana.
English Comments:
Threats
As for other finches, threats are probably now mainly introduced diseases.
Spanish Comments: Información adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: The smallest of all Darwin finches, about 8 grams, and the species with the thinnest beak.
Spanish Description: Es el pinzón más pequeño (aprox. 8 gramos) y con el pico más fino.

Author: Gould, 1837
Taxonomic Comments: This species is closely related to the Grey Warbler Finch, and were formerly considered conspecfic, but both species differ in appearance, distribution, habitat, and song. Syn.: Certhidea olivacea ridgwayi Rothschild & Hartert, 1899, Certhidea olivacea olivacea Gould, 1837, Certhidea olivacea mentalis Ridgway, 1894, Certhidea olivacea luteola Ridgway, 1894, Certhidea olivacea cinerascens Ridgway, 1890, Certhidea olivacea bifasciata Ridgway, 1894, Certhidea olivacea becki Rothschild, 1898.
Distribution Comments: C. olivacea is found on the larger central and western islands. Present on Pinzón, Fernandina, Isabela, Rabida, Santa Cruz, Santiago Islands.
English Comments:
Threats
Seems strongly affected by the parasitic introduced fly Philornis downsi, particularly in conjunction with heavy rainfall when parents are not able to feed the chicks extra to compensate for the blood loss. Pox prevalence was also found to increase for this species.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Al parecer está fuertemente afectado por la mosca parasita introducida Philornis downsi, particularmente en conjunto con las lluvias Fuertes cuando los padres no son capaces de sobre alimentar a los pichones para compensar la pérdida de sangre. También se encontró un incremento de la prevalencia de Viruela Aviar en esta especie.
English Description: The smallest of all Darwin finches, about 8 grams, and the species with the thinnest beak.
Spanish Description: Se trata del más pequeño de los pinzones de Darwin, aprox. 8 gramos, y con el pico más fino.

Author: Ridgway, 1894
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza difficilis  Sharpe, 1888; Geospiza difficilis debilirostris Ridgway, 1894; Geospiza difficilis difficilis Sharpe, 1888; Geospiza difficilis septentrionalis Rothschild & Hartert, 1899; Geospiza nebulosa (Gould, 1837).
Distribution Comments: Only in Genovesa Island.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Solo en la isla Genovesa.
English Description: Very similar to Vampire Ground-finch G. septentrionalis and Sharp-beaked Ground Finch G. difficilis.
Spanish Description: Muy parecido a pinzón vampiro G. septentrionalis y al pinzón de pico afilado G. difficilis.

Author: Ridgway, 1890
English Common Name: Large Cactus Finch, large cactus ground Finch
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza conirostris conirostris Ridgway, 1890; Geospiza conirostris darwini Rothschild & Hartert, 1899; Geospiza conirostris propinqua Ridgway, 1894
Distribution Comments: Espanola Island.
English Comments:
Threats
Appart from possible future introduction of diseases, there do not currently seem to be any serious threats, as Española and Genovesa are rat and Philornis free.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Con excepción de posibles introducciones futuras de enfermedades, no existe actualmente ninguna amenaza seria para la especie, pues Española y Genovesa son islas libres de ratas y Philornis.

Author: Sharpe, 1888
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza difficilis debilirostris Ridgway, 1894; Geospiza difficilis difficilis Sharpe, 1888; Geospiza difficilis septentrionalis Rothschild & Hartert, 1899; Geospiza nebulosa (Gould, 1837).
Distribution Comments: Present in the highlands of Santiago, Fernandina and Pinta, where the Small Ground Finch occupies the drier zones. In the present, in Darwin, Wolf is other species (G. septentrionalis), and in Genovesa (G. acutirostris). It is now extinct on Santa Cruz.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Se encuentra en las partes altas de Santiago, Fernandina y Pinta, donde el pinzón pequeño de tierra ocupa las zonas más secas. En la actualidad, en las islas Darwin y Wolf es otra especie (G. septentrionalis) y en Genovesa (G. acutirostris). Extincto de Santa Cruz.
English Comments:
Threats
Affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality, though data is missing.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Es afectado por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi que causa alta mortalidad de pichones, aunque se necesita más información.
Información adicional Venegas, L.
English Description:
Very similar to Vampire Ground-finch G. septentrionalis of Darwin and Wold, and Genovesa Ground-finch G. acutirostris.
Similar to the Small Ground-finch with slightly longer and more pointed beak, with its upper edge almost straight.
Spanish Description:
Muy parecido a pinzón vampiro G. septentrionalis de Darwin y Wolf, y al pinzón de tierra de Genovesa G. acutirostris.
Parecido al pinzón pequeño de tierra pero con el pico un poco más largo y puntiagudo, el borde superior más recto.

Author: Gould, 1837
Taxonomic Comments: Syn: Geospiza dubia (Gould, 1837); Geospiza dentirostris (Gould, 1837).
Distribution Comments: Widespread on all main islands except Darwin, Genovesa, and Wolf (where one was collected in 1906). In 1905-1906 fifteen non-breeding birds were collected on Española, but they may be stragglers or part of a now-extinct population.
Spanish Distribution Comments: En todas las islas mayores excepto Darwin, Genovesa, y Wolf (donde uno fue colectado en 1906). Entre 1905-1906, quince juveniles fueron colectados en Española, tal vez parte de una población ahora extinta.
English Comments:
Threats
Main threats are probably rats and disease. It is known to be affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Las principales amenazas probablemente son las ratas y enfermedades, se conoce que se encuentra afectado por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi que causa una alta mortalidad de pichones.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: In Santa Cruz, there are small beaked and large beaked birds; the latter can be confused with large ground finches, but beak depth is less and overall impression is smaller than large ground finch.
Spanish Description: En Santa Cruz, existen aves con picos pequeños y otros de pico grande que se pueden confundir con el pinzón grande de tierra. Sin embargo, los pinzones medianos de tierra tienen el pico menos alto y la impresión general al observar su pico no es tan masiva como al observar un pinzón grande de tierra.

Author: Gould, 1837
Distribution Comments: The species is present on all islands except Genovesa (possibly due to competition with the G. acutirostris), Darwin and Wolf (G. septentrionalis).
Spanish Distribution Comments: La especie se encuentra en todas las islas excepto Genovesa (posiblemente por competencia con el pinzón G. acutirostris), Darwin y Wolf (G. septentrionalis).
English Comments:
Threats
It is known to be affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality, and by avian pox. Introduced rats are probably the second cause of mortality.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Se conoce que se encuentra afectado por la mosca parasite Philornis downsi, la cual causa alta mortalidad de pichones, y por viruela aviar. Las ratas introducidas probablemente son la segunda causa de mortalidad.
Información adicional Venegas, L.

Author: Gould, 1837
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza strenua (Gould, 1837).
Distribution Comments: Listed by all the main islands except San Cristóbal (thought to be extinct), Darwin, and Española. However recent observations on San Cristóbal suggest the presence of some individuals. It is thought to be extinct on Floreana but is in the list of fossil species.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente en todas las islas mayores excepto San Cristóbal (posiblemente extincto), Darwin y Española. Sin embargo, observaciones recientes sugieren que algunos individuos se encuentran en San Cristóbal. Desapareció de Floreana pero consta en la lista de especies fósiles.
English Comments:
Threats
Affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi that causes heavy chick mortality, though data is missing.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
Es afectado por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi que causa alta mortalidad de pichones, sin embargo falta información.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.
English Description: The largest of ground finches,  approx. 35 g. Massive beak with the depth at the base about the same as its height. Upper mandible starts over the eye line.
Spanish Description: Es el más grande de los pinzones de tierra, approx. 35g. El pico es muy contundente, la base del mismo es tan grande como su largo completo. La mandíbula superior empieza más arriba de la línea de los ojos.

Author: Ridgway, 1894
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza scandens  (Gould, 1837); Geospiza scandens abingdoni (P. L. Sclater & Salvin, 1870); Geospiza scandens intermedia Ridgway, 1894; Geospiza scandens rothschildi Heller & Snodgrass, 1901; Geospiza scandens scandens (Gould, 1837); Cactornis scandens Gould, 1837; Cactornis assimilis Gould, 1837; Cactornis abingdoni (Sclater & Salvin, 1870).
Distribution Comments: Present only in Genovesa Island.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente solo en isla Genovesa.
English Description: Similar to Common Cactus Finch.
Spanish Description: Muy parecido a Pinzón de cactus comun.

Author: (Gould, 1837)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza scandens abingdoni (P. L. Sclater & Salvin, 1870); Geospiza scandens intermedia Ridgway, 1894; Geospiza scandens rothschildi Heller & Snodgrass, 1901; Geospiza scandens scandens (Gould, 1837); Cactornis scandens Gould, 1837; Cactornis assimilis Gould, 1837; Cactornis abingdoni (Sclater & Salvin, 1870).
Distribution Comments: Found on main islands except Fernandina and Pinzón (extinct ??).
Spanish Distribution Comments: Se encuentra en las islas grandes excepto Fernandina, Pinzón.
English Comments:
Threats
The species is increasingly affected by avian pox, although no evaluation of the impact on population exists. It is also affected by the parasitic fly Philornis downsi, but little data is available.
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
La especie esta progresivamente siendo más afectada por viruela aviar, aunque no existe una evaluación sobre su impacto real en las poblaciónes. Es también afectada por la mosca parásita Philornis downsi, pero existe muy poca información disponible al respecto.
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.

Author: Rothschild & Hartert, 1899
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Geospiza difficilis Sharpe, 1888; Geospiza difficilis debilirostris Ridgway, 1894; Geospiza difficilis difficilis Sharpe, 1888; Geospiza difficilis septentrionalis Rothschild & Hartert, 1899; Geospiza nebulosa (Gould, 1837).
Distribution Comments: Present in Darwin, Wolf.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Presente en Darwin, Wolf.
English Description: Similar to Sharp-beaked Ground Finch G. difficilis of Pinta, Fernandina and Santiago, and Genovesa Ground-finch G. acutirostris.
Spanish Description: Muy parecido a pinzón de pico afilado G. difficilis de Pinta Fernandina y Santiago, y al pinzón de tierra de Genovesa G. acutirostris.

Author: (Gould, 1837)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Camarhynchus crassirostris Gould, 1837; Camarhynchus variegatus (Sclater & Salvin, 1870).
Distribution Comments: All islands, except Santa Fe, Baltra, Seymour, Darwin, Wolf, Genovesa, Espanola.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Todas las islas, excepto Santa Fe, Baltra, Seymour, Darwin, Wolf, Genovesa, Espanola.
English Comments:
Threats
The main threat is probably introduced diseases and when populations are important there, the management of the agricultural areas (pesticide use, remaining forests etc).
Spanish Comments:
Amenazas
La mayor amenaza son probablemente las enfermedades introducidas y en los casos de zonas donde las poblaciones son importantes, el manejo de las áreas agrícolas (uso de pesticidas, bosques remanentes, etc.)
Infomación adicional Venegas, L.

Author: Linnaeus, 1766
Distribution Comments: It was intercepted in Baltra. This individual "boarded" an airplane in Quito accidentally. It arrived on Baltra alive, returned to Quito, but in this city, they were thought it was an endemic species of Galapagos and returned. It arrived a second time to Galápagos, but weak and died in the next day,

Author: Vieillot, 1808
Distribution Comments: A record on San Cristobal Island in 2012

Author: Gould, 1839
Taxonomic Comments: G. Jimenez-Uzcategui: "The taxonomy of this species has been very confusing: Ridgway (1896) mentions five species (considered even by most other authors of the time as subspecies): nanus, dubius, intercedens, carolensis, and abingdoni (the latter three of which he himself described). Two subspecies were recognized: P. r. nanus (Gould 1841), occurring on most islands, and P. r. dubius (Gould 1841), from San Cristóbal. Salvin (1876), but, suggested that specimens of P. r. dubius were instead juvenile males of P. r. nanus (Wiedenfeld 2006). However, the last study mitochondrial and nuclear genetic, data, morphology, and behavior suggest that Galápagos forms should be elevated to two full species: P. nanus Gould, 1838 (Galápagos Vermilion Flycatcher) and P. dubius Gould, 1839 (San Cristóbal Vermilion Flycatcher) (Carmi, etal. In press.)".
Distribution Comments: Restricted on San Cristóbal Island.

Author: Gould, 1838
Taxonomic Comments: G. Jimenez-Uzcategui: "The taxonomy of this species has been very confusing: Ridgway (1896) mentions five species (considered even by most other authors of the time as subspecies): nanus, dubius, intercedens, carolensis, and abingdoni (the latter three of which he himself described). Two subspecies were recognized: P. r. nanus (Gould 1841), occurring on most islands, and P. r. dubius (Gould 1841), from San Cristóbal. In press.)".
Distribution Comments: Breeds on most main islands except San Cristóbal (other species: P. dubius Gould, 1839) , Santa Fe, Rábida, Wolf, Española, Darwin, Genovesa, Baltra, because there are few or no recent records.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Se reproduce en la mayoria de las islas excepto en San Cristóbal (otra especie: P. dubius Gould, 1839) Santa Fe, Rábida, Wolf, Española, Darwin, Genovesa, Baltra, donde hay pocos o ningún registro
Spanish Comments: Infomación adicional Venegas, L.

Author: (Gould, 1839)
Distribution Comments: Common on all major islands but Genovesa. It is decreasing but still fairly common except on San Cristóbal where it is already rare.
Spanish Distribution Comments: Es una especie común en todas las islas grandes excepto Genovesa. Su abundancia parece disminuir y en la actualidad ya son escasos en San Cristóbal.
English Description: Largest flycatcher on the Galápagos, it is still a rather small member of its genus, only about 15-16 cm in length. Grey-brown, breast, grey throat, and male has yellow belly, female beige. May have a crest of feathers on top of the head. Rather thick beak.
Spanish Description: Es el tiránido más grande de Galápagos, sin embargo una especie bastante pequeña dentro de su género. 15 cm de largo. Pecho gris algo café, macho amarillento por debajo, la hembra es más gris.

Author: Linnaeus, 1758
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Ardea alba egretta Gmelin, 1789, Casmerodius albus (Linnaeus, 1758), Egretta alba (Linnaeus, 1758)
Distribution Comments: Isabela, Santa Cruz Islands.

Author: Bangs, 1903
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Ardea herodias Linnaeus, 1758; Ardea herodias Gould 1841
Distribution Comments: Breeds only on the main islands, usually in the coastal zones.

Author: Linnaeus, 1758
Distribution Comments: Present on Santa Cruz, San Cristobal, Isabela and Floreana

Author: (Linnaeus, 1758)
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Butorides striata (Linnaeus, 1758); Butorides striatus (Linnaeus, 1758). Wiedenfeld says: "Although this has at times been recognized as a separate species (Lava Heron), as pointed out by Payne (1974) the species limits are not clear and the Galapagos populations show no reliable species-level distinctions from continental B. striatus by plumage or morphology. Harris (1973) mentioned that in Galapagos are found birds breeding that resemble continental versions of B. striatus as well as many intergrades between those forms and Lava Heron. Further study is necessary to clarify the relationship of this subspecies and other members of the species" (Wiedenfeld 2006).

Author: Linnaeus, 1758
Distribution Comments:
Isabela, Fernandina, Santa Cruz
Last recorded 15/08/2014 in Playa de Los Perros, Santa Cruz, Island.

Author: Muller, 1776
Taxonomic Comments: Syn.: Hydranassa tricolor Muller, 1776
